summary: Defines FLUTE, a protocol for delivering files one-way over the Internet, especially suited to multicast networks. It builds on Asynchronous Layered Coding, the base protocol for massively scalable multicast distribution. It is an experimental protocol and was replaced by RFC 6726.

plainLanguage.summary: A radio tower sends the same song to everyone listening without asking each person. FLUTE sends files this way, and listeners cannot talk back.

subtitle: One-way file distribution to many receivers using multicast without replies

tldr.problem: Distributing large files to many receivers simultaneously requires a protocol that works over IP multicast, which is one-way only and cannot wait for each receiver to confirm it received the file.
tldr.mechanism: FLUTE (File Delivery over Unidirectional Transport) uses the ALC protocol as its base and adds a File Delivery Table (FDT) that tells receivers what files are being sent, how to find them, and how to decode them. Receivers use Forward Error Correction to reconstruct missing packets without asking the sender to resend.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now broadcast files to potentially thousands of receivers at once, making multicast practical for software updates, metadata distribution, and streaming file services. FLUTE was an experimental protocol and was updated in RFC 6726.

today: RFC 3926 is Experimental and has been superseded by RFC 6726, which provides an updated specification of FLUTE. The protocol remains in use for multicast-based file distribution in managed networks and research environments.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
FLUTE is a protocol for the unidirectional delivery of files over IP multicast networks. It builds on top of Asynchronous Layered Coding (ALC), which provides the basic transport mechanism for sending arbitrary binary objects to a group of receivers without requiring a return path or acknowledgments from any individual receiver.

The key innovation of FLUTE over bare ALC is that it adds a File Delivery Table (FDT) that is sent in-band along with the files themselves. The FDT tells receivers essential information about each file: its name, size, MIME type, content encoding, and cryptographic integrity checks. This lets applications automatically process received files without knowing in advance what would be sent.
sections.plainLanguage: ALC is like a radio broadcast—one speaker, many listeners. FLUTE adds labels that say 'this is a song,' 'this is a news report,' so listeners know what they're receiving.

sections.title: Target Applications and Limitations
sections.content:
FLUTE is designed for bulk delivery of large and small files to many hosts in a single session lasting several seconds or longer. Typical uses include software updates to thousands of machines, metadata distribution (such as SDP session descriptions), and subtitles or other time-lined data. The protocol leverages multicast's inherent scalability: a single sender can reach arbitrarily many receivers without increasing transmission rate.

However, FLUTE has important limitations. It cannot verify that receivers actually obtained the files; if reliable delivery verification is required, that must happen at the application level. FLUTE also works only in environments where multicast routing is available and receivers have some way to join a multicast group. In satellite or wireless networks with fixed transmission rates, rate-limiting may prevent some receivers from getting all FEC repair symbols, requiring careful protocol tuning.
sections.plainLanguage: FLUTE is great for sending a file to a million people at once, but the sender doesn't know if anyone actually got it. And it only works where multicast is allowed.

sections.title: How FLUTE Sessions Work
sections.content:
A FLUTE file delivery session is an ALC session containing both files and File Delivery Table instances. The sender assigns each file a unique Transport Object Identifier (TOI) and transmits both the file data and FDT packets over the same multicast address. Receivers reconstruct the FDT by collecting FDT packets (which use TOI = 0) and building a local FDT database of what files are available. Each FDT instance has an expiration time and an FDT Instance ID; receivers maintain a view of the FDT by receiving whichever FDT instances arrive.

Files themselves are identified by higher TOI values (1 and above). The sender can interleave packets from different files and different FDT instances arbitrarily. To aid receivers that join mid-session, the protocol recommends sending the FDT for a file before (or at least alongside) the file itself. Multiple FDT instances can describe the same files with the same parameters—effectively repeating the metadata for robustness—or provide incremental updates describing only new files.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender broadcasts 'here is file 1,' 'here is file 2,' mixed with 'file 1 is called picture.jpg and is 5 MB.' Receivers collect these labels into a list and grab the files they want.

sections.title: File Delivery Table (FDT) and Metadata
sections.content:
The FDT Instance is an XML structure sent as part of ALC packets. It must contain an Expires attribute (an NTP-based timestamp) showing how long the FDT is valid, and may contain a Complete attribute indicating that no future FDT instances will add new files. Each File element in the FDT must have a TOI (the transport object identifier) and a Content-Location (a URI identifying the file).

Optional attributes use MIME conventions: Content-Type (MIME type), Content-Length (original file size), Content-Encoding (compression algorithm), and Content-MD5 (hash for verification). For files that are content-encoded before transport, a separate Transfer-Length can specify the size after encoding. FEC parameters are also included so receivers know how the file is encoded for error correction.
sections.plainLanguage: The FDT is like a shipping label: file name, size, type, and a checksum so you can verify you got it right. All in standard email header format.

sections.title: Forward Error Correction and Repair
sections.content:
FLUTE inherits Forward Error Correction (FEC) capabilities from ALC. The sender encodes each file into FEC blocks, where each block is split into source symbols (the actual file data) and repair symbols (parity data calculated from the sources). By default, the sender transmits only source symbols; repair symbols are sent only in response to NACK (negative acknowledgment) requests from receivers.

When a receiver detects missing packets (by tracking sequence numbers), it can reconstruct missing symbols using FEC decoding if it has received enough other symbols. This allows scalable repair: instead of the sender repeating entire files, it sends a small amount of parity that any receiver experiencing loss can use to recover. The FEC encoding parameters are conveyed in-band either via an EXT_FTI header or within the FDT itself, so receivers always know how to decode.
sections.plainLanguage: If some packages get lost, the sender doesn't send the whole file again. Instead, it sends a math formula that lets receivers calculate what was missing, like a crossword puzzle clue.
